writingIdeas.viewpoint: Air-quality policy should target exposure, not only averages.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Citywide improvements can conceal severe pollution experienced by particular streets and groups.
writingIdeas.argument: A falling urban average may look successful even while schools beside major roads experience repeated peaks. Because health risk depends on where people spend time, fixed monitors should be supplemented by local and mobile measurements. Authorities can then redirect traffic, alter delivery times or improve filtration where exposure is greatest. This targeted approach uses evidence more fairly than applying an identical intervention everywhere. Success should be judged by whether the most exposed communities benefit, not simply by one citywide figure.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Clean transport zones need complementary support.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Restricting high-emission vehicles is effective only when households and businesses have realistic alternatives.
writingIdeas.argument: A charge can accelerate the replacement of polluting vehicles, but the immediate cost falls unevenly. A small business with one old van may struggle more than a large operator that routinely renews its fleet. Time-limited grants and reliable public transport can reduce that imbalance while preserving the incentive to change. Exemptions should remain narrow, or the environmental benefit will disappear. Combining a firm deadline with practical transition support is therefore both fairer and more likely to secure compliance.

speaking.question: Describe a place where you noticed poor air quality.
speaking.answer: I noticed it most clearly at a bus stop beside a wide road during the evening rush hour. Several buses and delivery vehicles were waiting with their engines running, and the air had a sharp smell that caught in my throat. What surprised me was how different it felt from a park only two streets away. I checked an air-quality app later, although its nearest monitor was quite distant, so it could not describe that exact corner. Since then, I have used a quieter parallel street when I walk home. The experience made air pollution feel local and immediate rather than like an abstract citywide statistic.

speaking.question: Should individuals change their routines when air pollution is high?
speaking.answer: Short-term precautions can be sensible, especially for children, older people and anyone with a respiratory condition. For instance, someone might exercise away from traffic or ventilate a room at a cleaner time of day. However, people cannot be expected to solve polluted air by constantly avoiding it. Many workers have fixed routes and hours, and not everyone can move home. Public authorities and major emitters therefore carry the main responsibility for reducing pollution at source, while clear advice helps residents manage unusual peaks.

reading.title: The Pollution Map Drawn by a School Day
paragraphs: Official monitors provide essential long-term records, but their small number can make pollution appear smoother than it is. A research team studying children’s exposure in one city therefore attached lightweight sensors to school bags. The aim was not to replace calibrated stations; it was to discover how pollution changed along the routes and indoor spaces that shaped an ordinary day.

The readings rose beside congested junctions and fell in streets separated from traffic by buildings. Yet distance alone did not explain the pattern. At one school, a playground set back from the road recorded short peaks when parents left engines running at the gate, while a classroom facing a quieter courtyard accumulated carbon dioxide because its windows remained closed. The study thus distinguished outdoor pollutants from poor ventilation, two problems requiring different remedies.

Personal sensors produce messy evidence. Movement, humidity and the position of a device can affect a reading, and children following different routes cannot be treated as a controlled laboratory sample. Researchers corrected the instruments against a fixed station and combined repeated journeys rather than interpreting one dramatic peak. The resulting map, while less precise at any single second, revealed consistent places where exposure increased.

Schools used the findings in varied ways. One changed the time at which delivery vehicles entered; another opened a walking entrance away from the main road. A third improved classroom ventilation after staff realised that keeping every window shut against traffic had created a separate indoor problem. None of these measures required families to abandon the neighbourhood.

The project’s larger lesson concerns measurement. An annual city average can show whether broad policy is working, whereas a child’s route reveals where practical protection is possible now. These forms of evidence are not competitors. Joined carefully, they connect regional emission controls with the small decisions—about gates, engines and windows—through which cleaner air becomes part of daily life.
